A table follows the light or dark look of the page it is shown in, with no code from you. When you
want to change more than that, a `Theme` is a reusable set of colors, fonts, and `~~GT.tab_options()`
values that you apply to one table with `~~GT.opt_theme()`. This page covers the automatic light and
dark behavior, how to write a theme, which value wins when several apply, the CSS variables that make
this work in HTML, and how to build a theme from a [brand.yml](https://posit-dev.github.io/brand-yml/)
file.

The examples use a small piece of `exibble`.

```{python}
from great_tables import GT, Theme, data

small = data.pl.exibble.select("num", "char", "currency", "row")

gt_small = GT(small, rowname_col="row").tab_header("A small table")
```

## Automatic Light and Dark

By default a table is in `"auto"` mode. It is light, and it turns dark when the page around it is
dark. It reads that from two places:

* The page's own theme, when the page is one of these hosts: JupyterLab and Notebook 7, VS Code
  notebooks, Quarto, marimo, or a page using Bootstrap 5.3's `data-bs-theme` attribute. When themes
  are nested, the nearest one wins, so a `data-bs-theme="light"` section of a dark page keeps its
  table light.
* The page's color scheme, the CSS `color-scheme` property. A page declares `dark` to be dark, or
  `light dark` to follow the reader's system setting. The pages that Great Tables makes (with
  `~~GT.show()` or `as_raw_html(make_page=True)`) declare `light dark`.

A page that says neither stays light, so a default table is never dark on a light page.

You do not need to do anything for this. The table below is a default table, so it changes with the
page it is shown in.

```{python}
gt_small
```

`~~GT.opt_theme()` takes a `mode=` to pin the table instead:

* `"light"`: always the light colors.
* `"dark"`: always the dark colors.
* `"auto"`: the default.

```{python}
gt_small.opt_theme(mode="dark")
```

```{python}
gt_small.opt_theme(mode="light")
```

Use `mode="dark"` for a table on a page that is always dark but doesn't say so, and `mode="light"`
for a table that should stay light on a dark page.

A table with a background color set through `~~GT.tab_options()` or `~~GT.opt_stylize()` stays light
in `"auto"` mode. Those colors were picked for a light table, and they apply in both modes, so
switching would give pale stripes on a dark table. `mode="dark"` still forces dark. The same goes for
a background option set in a `Theme`, unless the theme's `dark=` gives that option a value of its own:
then the table has a color for each mode, and it follows the page.

## Writing a Theme

A `Theme` holds values for a few tokens, plus any option that `~~GT.tab_options()` accepts. Give only
what you want to change. Everything else keeps its built-in value.

| Argument        | CSS variable               | What it sets                                                                  |
| --------------- | -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `background`    | `--gt-color-background`    | The table background. Sections without a color of their own use it.           |
| `foreground`    | `--gt-color-foreground`    | The text color on that background.                                            |
| `border`        | `--gt-color-border`        | The lines and borders that are light gray (`#D3D3D3`) by default.             |
| `border_strong` | `--gt-color-border-strong` | The top and bottom table borders.                                             |
| `stripe`        | `--gt-color-stripe`        | The background of striped rows.                                               |
| `accent`        | `--gt-color-accent`        | For your own CSS. Interactive tables' controls get it as `--gt-i-accent`.     |
| `font`          | `--gt-font-family`         | The font, one name or a list. It goes ahead of the default font stack.        |
| `font_size`     | `--gt-font-size`           | The base font size, as a CSS length or a number of pixels.                    |

Any other argument is the name of a `~~GT.tab_options()` option, checked the same way. An unknown
name raises an error.

A theme that sets `background` but not `foreground` keeps the built-in text colors, and the table
picks the light or the dark one for that background, as it does for
`~~GT.tab_options(table_background_color=...)`.

```{python}
compact = Theme(
    border="#9AA5B1",
    font="Georgia",
    data_row_padding="3px",
    column_labels_font_weight="bold",
)

gt_small.opt_theme(compact)
```

There are no tokens for spacing, since the default padding differs by table part. Set the padding
options (`data_row_padding`, `column_labels_padding`, and so on) in the theme instead.

### Colors for dark mode

`dark=` takes a second `Theme` with the values to use in dark mode. It can hold the five color tokens
(`background`, `foreground`, `border`, `border_strong`, `stripe`) and color options that are written
to the table's stylesheet, such as `table_body_hlines_color`. Anything else (a padding or a font, for
example) raises an error, because it cannot vary by mode in CSS. A `dark` theme cannot have its own `dark=`.

```{python}
navy = Theme(
    border="#9AA5B1",
    font="Georgia",
    dark=Theme(background="#101418", border="#2A3038"),
)

gt_small.opt_theme(navy)
```

The built-in dark theme supplies a background, text, border, strong border, and stripe color. A
theme's light color tokens are not used in dark mode. A theme that sets `background` and has no
`dark=` still goes dark with the built-in dark background, and `mode="light"` keeps it light. Spacing,
fonts, the accent, and any color option the theme sets directly carry over to dark mode unless
`dark=` replaces them. A border or line color that carries over is blended toward the dark text
color, since a color chosen for a light table (black lines, say) would barely show on a dark one. The
same is done for border colors set with `~~GT.tab_options()`. Give the option a value in `dark=` to
choose the dark color yourself.

## What Wins

When several things set the same option, the first of these that exists is used:

1. A value set with `~~GT.tab_options()` or an `opt_*()` method. It applies in both modes (a border
   color is blended in dark mode, as described above).
2. In dark mode, the option in the theme's `dark=`.
3. The option in the theme.
4. In dark mode, for an option fed by a color token: the token in the theme's `dark=`, then the
   built-in dark token.
5. The token in the theme.
6. The built-in value.

Setting an option to its default value with `~~GT.tab_options()` still counts as setting it.

Values from `~~GT.tab_options()` and the `opt_*()` methods are absolute. They are not scaled from the
theme. `~~GT.opt_vertical_padding()`, `~~GT.opt_horizontal_padding()`, and `~~GT.opt_table_font()`
with `add=True` compute from the built-in values, and what they compute then replaces the theme's
value. Below, the theme asks for `3px` of padding, and the `scale=2` in `opt_vertical_padding()`
doubles the built-in `8px`, so the rows get `16px`.

```{python}
gt_small.opt_theme(Theme(data_row_padding="3px")).opt_vertical_padding(scale=2)
```

The order of the calls does not matter. A theme is stored apart from the table's options, so
`~~GT.opt_theme()` before or after `~~GT.tab_options()` gives the same table.

## CSS Variables

In HTML, every option that is written to the table's stylesheet is a CSS variable on that table. The
name is `--gt-` followed by the option name, with underscores turned into hyphens: `data_row_padding`
is `--gt-data-row-padding`, and `table_body_hlines_color` is `--gt-table-body-hlines-color`. The
tokens use the names in the table above. These options are not part of the stylesheet and have no
variable: the footnote marks, order, and spec (`footnotes_marks`, `footnotes_order`,
`footnotes_spec_ref`, `footnotes_spec_ftr`); the source note separator and multiline setting
(`source_notes_sep`, `source_notes_multiline`); the container options (`container_width`,
`container_height`, `container_padding_x`, `container_padding_y`, `container_overflow_x`,
`container_overflow_y`); the Quarto options (`quarto_disable_processing`, `quarto_use_bootstrap`);
the options that say whether a part is included or shown (`table_border_top_include`,
`table_border_bottom_include`, `row_striping_include_stub`, `row_striping_include_table_body`,
`column_labels_hidden`, `row_group_as_column`); `table_id`, `table_caption`, and
`table_additional_css`; and the `ihtml_*` options. `table_font_names` has no variable of its own: it
is written through `--gt-font-family`.

`--gt-color-accent` is not read by any CSS. A static table has no accent, and an interactive table
reads `--gt-i-accent`: a theme's `accent` is written to that variable on the interactive table's
element, and page CSS can set `--gt-i-accent` itself.

A table declares a variable only for a value that was set from Python. Every other value is a
fallback in the CSS, so page CSS can set the variables on a parent of the table, and this works for
anything the Python code left alone. The page below sets a border color and tighter padding on every
table inside `.tight`.

```{=html}
<style>
.tight {
    --gt-color-border: #C0392B;
    --gt-data-row-padding: 2px;
}
</style>
```

::: {.tight}

```{python}
gt_small
```

:::

A value set from Python wins over the page's CSS, because the table declares it on its own element.
In the next table `data_row_padding` is set in Python, so the `2px` from the page CSS is not used,
while the border color from the page still is.

::: {.tight}

```{python}
gt_small.tab_options(data_row_padding="10px")
```

:::

The same holds for a theme: its values count as set from Python. A table cannot be restyled from page
CSS for any value its theme sets.

Custom properties are inherited. A table placed inside another table (for example, one pasted into a
cell as raw HTML) reads the variables that Python set on the outer table. The row details of
interactive tables are the exception: the outer table's variables are reset around them. That reset
also blocks page CSS, so a variable that the outer table sets does not reach a table in its row
details from the page either.

## brand.yml

If your organization describes its colors and fonts in a brand.yml file, `Theme.from_brand()` turns
it into a `Theme`. This needs the [brand_yml](https://pypi.org/project/brand-yml/) package, which is
installed with `pip install great_tables[brand]`. Without it, `Theme.from_brand()` raises an
`ImportError` that names the extra.

Take this `_brand.yml`.

```yaml
color:
  palette:
    navy: "#001F3F"
  background: "#FDF6E3"
  foreground: "#073642"
  primary: navy
typography:
  fonts:
    - family: Inter
      source: system
  base:
    family: Inter
    size: 14px
```

Pass its path to `Theme.from_brand()` and apply the result like any other theme.

```python
from great_tables import GT, Theme, data

theme = Theme.from_brand("_brand.yml")

GT(data.pl.exibble).opt_theme(theme)
```

These fields are used:

| brand.yml field          | `Theme` argument |
| ------------------------ | ---------------- |
| `color.background`       | `background`     |
| `color.foreground`       | `foreground`     |
| `color.primary`          | `accent`         |
| `typography.base.family` | `font`           |
| `typography.base.size`   | `font_size`      |

A color that names an entry of `color.palette` becomes that entry's color. A field the file does not
have is left out of the theme. The `border`, `border_strong`, and `stripe` tokens are not taken from
the brand, so they keep their built-in values. Font files and Google Font imports are not loaded; only
the family name is used.

A brand.yml file has one set of colors. For dark mode, pass a second file with `dark=`. Only its
`background` and `foreground` are used, as the colors of the theme's `dark=`.

```python
theme = Theme.from_brand("_brand.yml", dark="_brand-dark.yml")
```

Each argument can also be a `brand_yml.Brand` object. With no argument, `Theme.from_brand()` leaves
the search for a file to `brand_yml`. In `brand_yml` 0.2.0 that needs the `BRAND_YML_PATH`
environment variable to be set, so pass a path when you can.

## Limits

* **Colors you set on cells are not themed.** Literal colors from `~~GT.tab_style()`,
  `~~GT.data_color()`, and `~~GT.opt_stylize()` are written as you gave them, in both modes. A few
  cases are adjusted so the text stays readable:
    * A cell with a fill and no text color gets a text color chosen for contrast with the fill. In
      light mode this changes cells whose fill is dark or mid-tone (red, blue, or green, for example),
      not only dark fills. A text color you write with `style.css()` still wins.
    * A text color on a cell with no fill is blended toward the section's text color in dark mode, and
      is left as written in light mode.
    * A cell with both a fill and a text color is left as written, and so is a fill from
      `~~GT.data_color()` with its defaults.
    * A fill that is translucent or a keyword (`transparent`, `inherit`, and so on) is left alone.
    * `~~GT.data_color(autocolor_text=False)` fills keep the table's text color in light mode. In
      dark mode they get a text color chosen for contrast with the fill, so that light fills don't
      show the table's light text.
    * Border colors from `style.borders()` are blended toward the section's text color in dark mode,
      as text colors are.
    * Email HTML (`inline_css=True`) keeps the text and border colors you set as written, in both modes.
* **Forced dark can lower contrast.** In `mode="dark"`, text on a mid-tone fill that you set (the
  header of an `~~GT.opt_stylize()` table, for example) uses the dark theme's text color. It can have
  lower contrast than in light mode.
* **Content in a cell keeps its own colors.** Plots from extension packages, raw HTML or SVG, and
  images inside a cell are not adapted to dark mode.
* **`as_raw_html()` needs CSS custom properties.** Its output only renders as intended where the
  renderer supports them. `as_raw_html(inline_css=True)` writes literal styles instead, for one mode.
* **Some output has one mode.** Email HTML (`inline_css=True`), images, LaTeX, Word, and Typst output
  cannot follow a preference. In email HTML, `"auto"` gives the light table and `"dark"` the dark
  one. Output made through gridwell (`as_gridwell()`, and `gtsave()` to formats such as SVG or Word)
  and LaTeX ignores the mode and is light, even with `mode="dark"`; the theme values those outputs
  can express, such as border colors, still apply.
* **Quarto renders use literal styles unless the format is HTML.** HTML shown in a Quarto render is
  written the same way as email HTML when the format is not HTML, and for any format when Quarto
  does not report it (older Quarto versions).
* **Iframes and shadow roots do not see the host's theme.** A table in a shadow root follows the
  color scheme it inherits from the page, and a table in an iframe follows the color scheme of the
  iframe's own page (light, if that page does not declare one).
* **Other dark pages get a light table.** Colab and Databricks give no theme signal. Sites built with
  Sphinx or MkDocs may have a dark theme of their own, but the table follows it only if the theme
  sets `color-scheme`. Add `color-scheme: dark` to the page's dark CSS, or use `mode="dark"` if the
  page is always dark.
* **Older browsers show the light table.** Switching needs CSS `light-dark()` (in browsers since
  2024); in a browser without it, an `"auto"` table is always light.
